input.question: Why is methionine always the "start" codon for proteins?
input.ground_truth: Interestingly, AUG is actually not the only start codon, though it is by far the most popular. [Alternative start codons](_URL_0_) include GUG and UUG. The most interesting thing is that these alternative codons are still translated as Met, regardless of what they typically code for, by using a special start codon tRNA. So, we come back to the same question: why Met? As far as I can tell, nobody really knows.

Now, proteins are built using little pieces called "amino acids." But how does your cell know when to start building a new protein tower? That's where the "start codon" comes in! A codon is like a special code made of three building blocks (letters) from the instructions.

Out of all the possible codes, the code "AUG" (which tells the cell to use the amino acid called methionine) is chosen as the "start" code. This is because:

- When the cell sees "AUG," it knows, "Okay, time to start building a new protein tower, and the first block will be methionine."
- Methionine is a special block that helps hold the tower together at the beginning.
- Also, the machinery that builds proteins is set up to start when it sees "AUG," so it’s like a magic word that tells everyone to get ready!

So, every time your body wants to build a new protein, it starts with methionine because "AUG" is the special starting code!
